question: A load draws 10 A RMS from 230 V RMS. Can you be sure it uses 2300 W?
options: Yes, P = V x I always
Only if it is a motor
No: if current and voltage are out of step, the real power is less than V x I
No: it always uses more than V x I
explanation: V_rms x I_rms is the apparent power. Real power is V_rms x I_rms x cos(phi), which equals it only when the current is in phase with the voltage.

question: What is the average power taken by an ideal inductor connected to a sine-wave source?
options: Zero: it stores energy for a quarter cycle and gives it back the next
V_rms x I_rms
Infinite
Exactly half of V_rms x I_rms
explanation: With a 90 degree phase shift, p(t) = v x i is positive and negative for equal times, so the average is zero.

question: A motor draws 11.5 A RMS from 230 V with the current lagging by 36.87 degrees (cos = 0.8). What is the real power?
explanation: P = 230 x 11.5 x 0.8 = 2116 W. 2645 VA is the apparent power and 1587 var the reactive power.

question: Why does a poor power factor matter if the reactive energy is returned every cycle?
options: It does not matter at all
Reactive power is billed as if it were heat in the load
It makes the voltage frequency drift
The extra current still flows in the wires, transformers and generators and heats them (I^2 R)
explanation: The supply must carry the full current, whatever part of it does useful work, and wire losses depend on current squared.

question: How is complex power computed from RMS phasors?
options: S = V x I
S = V / I
S = V x conj(I)
explanation: S = V conj(I): the conjugate subtracts the current's angle, so the angle of S is phi, and its real and imaginary parts are P and Q.

question: What is the usual way to correct a lagging power factor caused by motors?
options: Add a capacitor in parallel with the motor
Add a resistor in series with the motor
Add an inductor in parallel with the motor
Raise the supply frequency
explanation: A parallel capacitor supplies reactive power of the opposite sign, so the energy sloshes locally between motor and capacitor instead of travelling along the line.

question: After adding the right correction capacitor, which current changes?
options: The motor current drops to zero
The line current (between supply and capacitor) drops; the motor current stays the same
Both the motor current and the line current double
Nothing changes; only the bill does
explanation: The motor still sees the same voltage and draws the same current and real power. Only the supply side carries less current, because it no longer delivers the reactive part.
